headline: SoftBank se arrepiente de no invertir en Anthropic y sus acciones caen 16%
summary: Masayoshi Son, fundador de SoftBank, dijo esta semana que lamenta no haber respaldado a Anthropic. La firma ya había comprometido su apoyo a su rival OpenAI, donde ahora ha invertido 64.600 millones de dólares. El viernes, día después de la histórica salida a bolsa de Anthropic, las acciones de SoftBank cayeron hasta un 16% en Tokio. Si la pérdida se mantiene, sería el peor día de la empresa en más de dos años, según CNBC. La acción ronda ahora un tercio de su máximo de junio. La debut de Anthropic no impulsó al resto del sector IA. El Nasdaq cayó más de un 2% el jueves, y el mercado de Taiwán se encamina a su peor semana desde 1991. El arrepentimiento de Son pone de relieve la volatilidad del mercado de IA, donde las apuestas por una empresa u otra pueden marcar la diferencia entre ganancias millonarias y pérdidas abultadas. Mientras tanto, Anthropic consolida su posición como una de las principales empresas de frontera en inteligencia artificial, con una valoración que refleja el apetito de los inversores por el sector. headline: One Coding Plan, Three API Protocols: How to Choose the Right AI Coding Client Setup
summary: If you already use Claude Code, Codex, Kimi Code, OpenCode, or another configurable coding agent , this guide shows how to choose the correct protocol before you touch a config file. AceDataCloud’s current Coding Plan starts at a ¥99 CNY display price for 30 days . The entry tier includes 400 base Credits plus a 100-Credit limited-time bonus through November 30, 2026 . The important detail is what the plan is—and is not. It is a time-limited, usage-metered multi-model API package, not an official Claude, ChatGPT, or other consumer membership. Credits are deducted according to model usage, including relevant input, output, and cache operations. Start with the client’s protocol, not the model name Most integration failures happen because three separate choices get mixed together: Client : the terminal or IDE tool you work in. Protocol : the request/response format the client sends. Model : the model identifier selected for a task. AceDataCloud currently exposes three practical routes for coding workflows: Protocol route Best starting point Typical client/workflow Claude Messages A client designed around Anthropic Messages Claude Code OpenAI Responses An agent built around the Responses API Codex workflows OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions A client that accepts a custom OpenAI-style provider Kimi Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw, Aider, Cline, and similar tools This distinction prevents a common mistake: choosing a model first and assuming every client can call it through every protocol. A model may be in the current Coding catalog while a particular client still requires a specific provider format. Use the Coding Plan configuration center to find the guide for your exact client. Treat its endpoint, environment-variable, and model-name examples as one configuration unit; do not combine the base URL from one protocol with the request body from another. A minimal protocol smoke test Before debugging an agent, verify the credential and endpoint with the smallest possible request. The following example uses an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions route. Replace both placeholders with a Coding credential and a model ID currently shown for that credential: export ACEDATA_API_KEY = ' ' export ACEDATA_MODEL = ' ' curl --fail-with-body \ https://api.acedata.cloud/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACEDATA_API_KEY" \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d "{ \"model\": \"$ACEDATA_MODEL\", \"messages\": [ {\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"Reply with exactly: protocol-ok\"} ], \"stream\": false }" This is a configuration example, not a claim of a benchmark. A successful JSON response verifies four things at once: DNS/TLS access, credential acceptance, route compatibility, and recognition of the selected model. It does not prove that a full coding agent is configured correctly. If it fails, diagnose by status code before changing random settings: 401 : check the placeholder was replaced and that the Coding credential—not an unrelated key—is being used.

headline: Private conversations with AI may have been exposed due to provider issues
summary: OpenRouter removed three AI hosting providers and revoked Zero Data Retention eligibility for 125 endpoints after research uncovered policy violations where test prompts were improperly handled or copied across providers. headline: FreshGauge: a freshness control plane inside the LLM gateway
summary: Every LLM answer is a snapshot of the model's training data. Ask for a price, a current model name, a CEO, or a fine cap and you get something that was true — stated with exactly the same confidence as something that still is. Retrieval doesn't fix this on its own: RAG grounds an answer in documents, but nobody checks whether the document the answer leans on is two years old. FreshGauge is a Bifrost gateway plugin that does that check on the way out. Every completion that passes through the gateway gets its factual claims extracted, verified against live web evidence, scored by authority-weighted recency , and then acted on — logged, corrected in flight, or pre-empted with a dated brief before the model is even called. This is a write-up of how it's built, the decisions that mattered, and the traps that cost real debugging time. 1. Why the gateway is the right place You could build this as a wrapper around one SDK. It breaks the moment a team uses three providers, streams tokens, or fails over between models. A gateway sees all of that by construction: one process, one config, every request. Bifrost's plugin ABI gives exactly the hooks needed: PostLLMHook — the response, after the provider call. Where the audit is born. HTTPTransportPreHook — every HTTP request to the gateway. Where the audit API lives. Because HTTPTransportPreHook runs after Bifrost's auth, the plugin's admin routes inherit virtual-key auth for free. There is no second auth system to get wrong. 2. Architecture ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐ client ──POST─────────▶│ Bifrost gateway (:8080) │ /v1/chat/completions │ │ │ HTTPTransportPreHook ──▶ /audit, /stats, … │ │ │ (auth'd by VK) │ │ ▼ │ │ provider call (OpenAI / Anthropic / X / …) │ │ │ │ │ PostLLMHook │ └────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ 1. extract claims (≤8) │ 2. correct in flight? ◀── ledger read (0 credits) │ 3. dedupe by request/content ▼ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ auditor (2 workers) │ │ per claim: │ │ Tavily search ────┼──▶ api.tavily.com (1–2 credits) │ fetch + quote │ │ stance: +1 / −1 / 0│ │ vote = auth·e^(−age/τ) └──────────┬───────────┘ ▼ ┌──────────────────────┐ │ SQLite ledger │ │ audits · claims · │ │ evidence · metrics │ └──────────┬───────────┘ ▼ GET /audit/{id}.html (flat paper report) GET /stats (corrections, grounded) Three modes sit on one engine: Mode When Cost What the user sees shadow after the answer Tavily credits nothing; the ledger only correct inside PostLLMHook 0 credits (ledger read) dated correction block appended brief in HTTPTransportPreHook 1 Tavily search answer born current The cost asymmetry is the point. Detection needs the web. Enforcement does not — it needs the memory of what was already detected. 3. Claim extraction The extractor pulls sentences that make checkable assertions about the world and classifies them: const ( Pricing Category = "pricing" APIVersion Category = "api_version" Leadership Category = "leadership" Regulation Category = "regulation

headline: Your MCP server costs money to run. Here's how to charge for it.
summary: Every call to your MCP server costs you something. Maybe it's an LLM call, a GPU minute, a scraping proxy, or a paid API you're reselling. When the caller was a human clicking a button, that was fine. Now the caller is an agent in a loop, and it can call your tool 400 times before lunch. At some point you have to charge for it. This post walks through the three ways to do that today, with the code and the failure modes for each: Build it yourself — API keys and a balance in your own database. x402 — the agent pays per request, on-chain. A clearinghouse — a gateway handles keys, wallets, and billing, and you verify signed requests. I'll be upfront: I co-built a clearinghouse, Nexus402 , so option 3 is the one I know best. But I'll give you everything you need to do option 1 properly, because for some tools it's the right answer. What "charge per tool call" actually requires Before picking an approach, here's the checklist. Every option has to answer all of these somehow: Who is calling? You need a stable identity per paying customer. What does this call cost? A price per tool, known before the call runs. Can they pay? Check the balance before doing the expensive work, not after. Charge exactly once. Agents retry. Networks drop responses. A retry must never become a second charge. What if you fail? If your server times out or throws, should the caller still pay? Stop runaway spend. A buggy agent loop shouldn't empty someone's wallet in ten minutes. Get paid. Money has to actually reach your bank account. The trap most people fall into is post-paid metering : log usage, invoice at the end of the month. It's easy to build and it's the wrong default for agents. You do the expensive work first and find out weeks later whether the card works. Prepaid balances flip that around: no balance, no call. Option 1: Build it yourself You issue API keys, keep a prepaid balance per customer, and debit it on every call. The core of it is one atomic database statement. The schema CREATE TABLE accounts ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY , api_key_hash BYTEA NOT NULL UNIQUE , -- store a hash, never the key balance_micro BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK ( balance_micro >= 0 ) ) ; CREATE TABLE charges ( account_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts ( id ) , idempotency_key TEXT NOT NULL , tool TEXT NOT NULL , amount_micro BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK ( amount_micro > 0 ) , status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'charged' , -- charged | refunded created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now ( ) , PRIMARY KEY ( account_id , idempotency_key ) ) ; Two decisions are doing the work here: Money is an integer count of micro-dollars ( BIGINT ), never a float. $0.02 is 20000 . Floats will eventually turn 0.1 + 0.2 into a billing dispute. CHECK (balance_micro >= 0) makes overdraft impossible at the database level, even if your application code has a bug. headline: Building a Lightweight Windows AI Agent with Nature AI Worker
summary: Introduction AI agents that can read, write, and analyze files locally are increasingly useful for developers and data workers. However, many AI tools require complex setups involving Python, Docker, or administrator rights, which can be barriers for quick experimentation or lightweight use. Nature AI Worker is an open-source Windows application designed to provide a simple, standalone AI agent interface. It connects to supported local Ollama models and cloud AI provider APIs without requiring Python, Git, WSL, Docker, or admin rights. This article explains the concepts behind such AI agents, the trade-offs involved, and how to get started with it. Understanding AI Agents and Tool Calling An AI agent is a system that can perform tasks autonomously by interacting with tools or data sources. Unlike a simple chatbot, an agent can read files, search data, perform calculations, and write results back to disk. Tool Calling Tool calling means the AI model can invoke external functions or tools during its reasoning process. For example, it might call a file search tool to find relevant documents or a calculator to perform exact arithmetic. This capability extends the AI's usefulness beyond text generation. An agent that works through tools needs a model that supports tool calling. For local Ollama models, that means a tool-capable model such as qwen3 or llama3.1 . Trade-offs in Lightweight AI Agent Design Pros No complex dependencies: No need for Python, Docker, or admin rights. Standalone installer: Easy to install and run on Windows. User control: File changes and web fetches wait for your approval, so you decide when they happen. Supports multiple providers: Works with OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Ollama, and OpenAI-compatible APIs. Cons Single-user, local use: Not designed for multi-user or enterprise deployments. No shell or code execution: The agent is limited to its file, table and arithmetic tools. Early release: The v0.1.1 installer does not include an enterprise platform client. No guaranteed latency or privacy: Network calls and data handling depend on the provider. Setting Up Nature AI Worker Installation Download the v0.1.1 Windows installer from the GitHub repository . The installer needs no Python, Git, WSL, Docker or administrator rights. Configuration After installation, configure your AI model provider: For local Ollama models, ensure you have a tool-capable model like qwen3 or llama3.1 installed. For cloud providers, enter your API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, or others supported. Workspace The app uses a single workspace folder where the built-in General Agent can read, search, and write files. Place your data files (CSV, TSV, JSON) here for analysis. Using the General Agent The built-in General Agent can: Read and summarize CSV, TSV, and JSON tables. Perform exact arithmetic calculations. Search files within the workspace. headline: A Raw Neural Network Is Not an AI Brain: Architecting an 8-Floor Cognitive System, 12 Firewall Tunnels, and a Rover on Mars
summary: Stop everything and keep your terminal open, because I am opening the forensic black box of an 8-floor cognitive software architecture. Before we inspect a single equation or Python module, let’s set the baseline straight: I am not an academic researcher with three MIT degrees framed on my wall. I am forty-four years old, I left traditional schooling after the ninth grade, and fifteen corporate doors stayed shut in my face without so much as an automated reply. I curse when a language server crashes at 6:00 AM, I second-guess myself late at night, and after twenty-three straight hours awake, my eyes blur until three log lines look like one. Yet when you run a deterministic parser across my raw, SHA-256-sealed trajectory logs ( transcript.jsonl ) from six consecutive days of engineering without a safety net—documented in Volume IV of my open-access monograph on CERN/Zenodo —the disk telemetry speaks for itself: ▸ 9,394 execution steps & 4,898 tool calls: Logged deterministically across six continuous days of systems engineering. ▸ 69,825 words typed by hand: Including 50,706 words in 72 hours —the exact word count of a 200-page book of live architectural constraints, AST rules, and bug reports typed from my desk in Montreal. ▸ The +0.38% Metronomic Constant: 103.8 steps/hour on Saturday (16.66h) versus 104.2 steps/hour on Monday (12.18h right after a 23.23-hour sleepless Sunday sprint), while mean prompt density held steady at 259.2 vs. 257.7 words/prompt (-0.58% variance across 72 hours!). Why publish every metric, failure audit, and blueprint across 55 Open-Proof folders instead of hiding behind 2023-style NDAs? Because Harvard Business School’s study on open-source value uncovered a 2,120x economic leverage multiplier ($8.80T in siloed demand value vs. $4.15B supply cost), where 96% of global value comes from 5% of builders . headline: The Future of QA in 2026: Why Quality Engineers Are Becoming AI-Powered Quality Strategists
summary: Introduction For years, Quality Assur__ance (QA) was often viewed as the final checkpoint before software releases. Teams wrote test cases, executed regressions, logged defects, and signed off on deployments. That reality is changing rapidly. With AI generating code, businesses releasing updates multiple times a day, and customers expecting flawless digital experiences, traditional testing approaches are no longer enough. Modern organizations are moving from Quality Assurance (QA) to Quality Engineering (QE), where quality is embedded throughout the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). The biggest driver behind this transformation? Artificial Intelligence and Agentic Testing. Industry reports and QA trend analyses indicate that AI is becoming deeply integrated into software engineering and testing workflows, while organizations increasingly adopt AI-assisted testing, autonomous test generation, and continuous quality practices. Let’s explore the key QA trends that are shaping the future of software testing. AI-Powered Testing Is Becoming the New Standard AI is no longer just a buzzword in testing. Modern testing platforms can now: Generate test cases automatically Identify high-risk modules Detect flaky tests Self-heal test scripts Recommend regression coverage Analyze production failures Instead of spending hours maintaining automation scripts, QA engineers can focus on exploratory testing, risk analysis, and business validation. Organizations embracing AI-powered quality engineering are seeing faster release cycles and improved productivity. AI-generated code and tests are also becoming more common, creating a growing need for robust verification strategies. What this means for QA professionals Future QA engineers must learn: Prompt engineering AI-assisted test generation Test validation strategies AI governance and risk assessment The question is no longer: “Can AI test software?” The real question is: “How effectively can humans validate what AI produces?” Agentic Testing Is the Next Big Revolution One of the most exciting developments in 2026 is Agentic Testing. Unlike traditional automation tools that follow predefined scripts, AI agents can: Understand requirements Generate complete test scenarios Execute tests autonomously Analyze failures Suggest fixes Industry experts describe agentic testing as a major shift where AI moves from being a testing assistant to becoming an active quality partner. Imagine telling an AI: “Validate the checkout journey for a premium customer using multiple payment methods.” The AI automatically creates, executes, analyzes, and reports test results. This is no longer science fiction. It’s happening now. headline: Muru – AI-assisted Rust server for Python apps by mod_WSGI's creator
summary: Muru Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since. Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production. As he did with wrapture , he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process. Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks: 2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next 2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru 2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers 2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together 2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many 2026-11-10 — Muru: HTTPS in development 2026-11-11 — Muru: WSGI and ASGI together 2026-11-11 — AI as a lifestyle choice 2026-11-12 — Muru: releases, not restarts 2026-11-13 — Muru: canaries without a service mesh 2026-11-14 — Muru: a better tenant in a container 2026-11-15 — Muru: working with Kubernetes, not around it 2026-11-16 — Muru: scaling from what the workers report 2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero 2026-11-18 — Muru: overlays on a schedule 2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding 2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page 2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read: The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too. headline: What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)? A Business Owner's Guide
summary: If you have looked into adding AI to your business, you have probably hit a frustrating limitation early on: a general AI chatbot knows nothing about your company. Ask it about your products, your prices, or your internal procedures, and it will either admit ignorance or, worse, confidently invent an answer. The technology that solves this problem is called retrieval-augmented generation , or RAG. It is the architecture behind most serious business AI assistants today, and understanding it will make you a much smarter buyer of AI solutions. The problem: language models have no knowledge of your business A large language model like the ones behind ChatGPT or Claude is trained on a broad snapshot of public text. It can write, summarize, translate, and reason impressively well, but its knowledge has two hard limits: It only knows what was in its training data. Your internal documents, your current price list, and your customer records were not there. It cannot look things up on its own. Left alone, it generates the most plausible-sounding answer, whether or not it is true. In a business context, a confident wrong answer about your return policy or a medication dosage is a serious problem. Training a custom model on your data sounds like the obvious fix, but it is expensive, slow to update, and still cannot cite where an answer came from. RAG takes a different, more practical route. How RAG works, in plain terms RAG combines a search system with a language model. Instead of asking the AI to answer from memory, the system first retrieves the relevant facts, then asks the AI to write an answer based on those facts. The flow looks like this: Indexing: Your documents, such as product catalogs, FAQs, manuals, contracts, and procedures, are split into small chunks and stored in a searchable database built for meaning-based search, not just keyword matching. Retrieval: When a user asks a question, the system searches that database and pulls out the handful of chunks most relevant to the question. Generation: The question and the retrieved passages are given to the language model together, with instructions to answer using only the provided material, and ideally to cite which document the answer came from. The result is an assistant that answers questions about your business, in natural language, with answers grounded in your documents. When your price list changes, you update the document, not the model. New information is live as soon as it is indexed. Where RAG delivers value Customer support assistants that answer from your actual policies and product data instead of generic guesses Internal knowledge assistants that let employees ask questions across years of procedures, contracts, and project documents in seconds Technical documentation help for complex products, where correct answers exist but are buried in hundreds of pages Sales enablement tools that draft responses to prospect questions using your approved materials What separates a good RAG system

headline: I Let My AI Agent Enter 11 Paid Bounties in One Day — Here's What Happened
summary: This weekend I pointed my AI coding agent at make.fun, a platform that runs paid build bounties — chess engines, games, solvers, data tools — where entries are built by AI agents and the best ones get paid in USDC on Solana. One day later, the agent had 11 entries submitted and accepted across 10 different bounties. No copy-pasting code into forms — the agent researched each bounty, built in a real repo, ran the platform's local checks, and submitted on its own. What it entered A 4 KB chess engine — practice Elo ~1,364–1,545, safely above the 1,154 final cutoff A Sokoban solver — a perfect practice score of 1,000,000 / 1,000,000, then a v2 that shaved ~1.5 KB off the solution (size is the tie-breaker) A GTA 6 fan game ("Port Solano: Sunset City") — day cycle, traffic, pedestrians, missions, police roadblocks A stealth game and a heist game — both passed local checks 16/16 A tiny stack VM — 40/40 byte-exact on practice, another perfect grade A token launch radar — the biggest pool of the batch ($1,325), open until Dec 14 Two daily news-in-one-image entries and a broken-CSV speed reader Total prize pools across those bounties: several thousand dollars. First results land December 7. What actually made it work Three lessons from watching an agent do this end-to-end: Read the checks before you build. Every bounty publishes machine-checked requirements. The agent that reads them first wastes zero submissions; the one that guesses gets rejected. Score locally, submit once. Each bounty ships a local grader. We never submitted anything that hadn't already passed at home. Newest submission counts. On resubmission-friendly bounties, a better v2 replaces v1 — so the agent kept improving entries while the windows were open instead of stopping at "good enough." Try it with your own agent If you have a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, anything that can work in a repo), make.fun is genuinely one of the most interesting proving grounds right now: real specs, real graders, real USDC. Join with my referral link: https://make.fun/r/agz5j45q Full disclosure: it's a referral link. If an account that signs up through it wins a bounty, make.fun pays me a 10% bonus on top for 90 days — it never comes out of the winner's prize. The referred account earns nothing extra from the link, so use it only if you're fine with that. Results start dropping December 7. I'll post a follow-up with what the 11 entries actually earned — win or lose, the numbers will be real. — bayu29 on make.fun

headline: Can you sell unused AI API credits? Two checks before they expire
summary: An API dashboard shows $100 left and an expiry date three weeks away. How much could you earn from that balance? To answer, you need two details the dashboard usually leaves out: what your agreement allows and how much usage will actually count toward settlement. 1. Check what you can supply Start with the agreement for the specific resource you hold. For example, the AWS Promotional Credit Terms prohibit selling promotional credits. The OpenAI Services Agreement prohibits buying, selling, or transferring API keys to third parties. A channel appearing in a supplier portal does not establish that your individual account qualifies. If you operate under a separate commercial agreement, check whether it permits the way you intend to supply the resource. If the wording is unclear, describe the arrangement to your provider and ask for confirmation. The provider name and credit type are enough to start that conversation. Keep the key itself private. 2. Calculate earnings from accepted usage For eligible resources on APIKEY, multiply the dollar value of accepted usage by the supplier rate locked for that resource. Settlement is in USDT on the TRC20 network. Suppose $100 is available and your hypothetical rate is 0.50 USDT per dollar. If $40 of usage is accepted before expiry, you earn 20 USDT . If only $10 is accepted, you earn 5 USDT . When comparing offers, check the rate’s units, the expiry date, and the amount of usage actually accepted. The same starting balance can produce very different payouts. If you have eligible unused AI API credits you want to sell, create an account to see supported channels and rates . headline: The AI purple is a 2017 gradient called Plum Plate
summary: You've seen this one. If you've opened a vibe-coded landing page in the last year or so, there's a good chance its hero was linear-gradient(135deg, #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100%) , with white text on top. GitHub's code search finds #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100% in about 1.3 million files. The agent skill packs have noticed: ECC 's generator agent says "#667eea -> #764ba2 is an instant tell", and Impeccable 's slop detector counts both as AI purples. The usual explanation for AI going purple is Tailwind , whose creator Adam Wathan half-apologised in August 2025 for making every Tailwind UI button bg-indigo-500 . But this isn't a Tailwind colour. It's Plum Plate, number 28 of the 180 swatches in WebGradients , a free gallery itmeo put out in January 2017. And for most of its life, hardly anyone used it. Nobody wanted it for eight years Stack Overflow has 17 posts with both colours in from 2017 to 2022. Over the same years, the old Flat UI blue, #3498db , is in 1,314. In a 2022 snapshot of GitHub with 470,000 HTML files in it, Plum Plate is in one, and #3498db is in 121. The first wave of chatbots didn't go for it either. WildChat is 838,000 real ChatGPT conversations from April 2023 to April 2024, and ChatGPT wrote Plum Plate in one of them. LMArena's public dumps from 2023 to summer 2024, the last one with Claude 3 and 3.5 Sonnet in, have it zero times. Then Claude 4 came out Claude Sonnet 4 and Opus 4 launched on 22 May 2025. LMArena's next dump has 271,000 answers from April to July 2025, so I took every answer that wrote a CSS gradient and checked how many were this one: How often a model's CSS gradient was Plum Plate, April to July 2025 ( the data ) Answers in LMArena's arena-human-preference-140k that write a linear-gradient . Thinking variants are counted with their model. That's 93 of Claude 4's 232 gradients, against 20 of 670 for other companies' models. 83 of Claude's 93 are the line from the top of this post, word for word, and they start on cue: two Plum Plate answers in April from anyone, then 29 in May. Why Claude 4 took this one out of 180, I've no idea. It took a second one too: Ripe Malinka, number 17, a pink one, turns up 12 times in Claude 4's answers (a couple as extra stops on the end of Plum Plate) and twice in everyone else's. Keep that name in mind for the next bit. Then it was all over GitHub Count GitHub's hits for every two-colour swatch in WebGradients, and it's barely a contest: GitHub code-search hits for WebGradients' 123 two-colour swatches ( the data ) Exact-string searches like #667eea 0%, #764ba2 100% , one per swatch, 20 November 2026. GitHub calls these totals estimates. Plum Plate is 69% of the lot, 11 times the runner-up, and the runner-up's Ripe Malinka. The median swatch gets 609. Hit counts don't say when the files were written, so I took the first 100 CSS files the search gives for Plum Plate and found the commit that added the line to each. 95 were added in 2025 or 2026. headline: Full-duplex speech isn't a faster pipeline — it's a policy you have to own
summary: The myth goes like this: full-duplex speech-to-speech is what you get when you make the ASR → LLM → TTS chain fast enough that the seams stop showing. Same pipeline, better plumbing. It's a comforting story, because it means adopting the new thing is an infrastructure upgrade — swap the components, keep the architecture, ship on Friday. That's not what it is. Haru-4B and the small crop of models like it aren't a faster version of the thing I already run. They move the hardest decision in a voice agent out of my config file and into a set of weights. That decision is: who speaks next, and when. The knob I've spent too many afternoons turning I've shipped VAD thresholds. Everyone who's shipped a voice agent has. You pick 300ms of trailing silence because 200 cuts people off mid-thought and 500 makes the assistant feel like it's buffering on a bad connection. Then a user pauses before the important part of the sentence, the assistant jumps in with "Sure, I can help with that," and the user has to start over. So you bump it to 400. Now the assistant feels sluggish, and your latency dashboard — the one you were so proud of — is green the whole time, because the VAD isn't in your latency budget. It's in the gap between the numbers you measure and the experience people have. Then someone says "mm-hm" while the assistant is mid-answer. That's not speech and it's not silence. It's a backchannel. Your threshold has no category for it, so your barge-in logic does one of two things: ignores it (the user feels unheard) or kills a perfectly good answer (the user feels punished for being polite). You patch it with a minimum-word-count heuristic and a blacklist, and now you're maintaining a tiny, bad, hand-written model of human conversational rhythm. Full-duplex systems fold that whole mess into the model. Audio in, audio out, continuously, with the model deciding when to yield, when to overlap, when to keep going through a "mm-hm." Architecturally that's the right answer. It's also not a knob. A learned policy is not a threshold This is the part of the myth that actually costs money. You cannot turn a learned turn-taking policy down from 0.4 to 0.3 when support forwards you a complaint. There's no dial. There's a distribution the model learned from, and either your users live in it or they don't. And you can't measure it against a public benchmark, because turn-taking is a property of your traffic, not of English. Some user populations overlap constantly and treat interruption as engagement. Some wait for a beep. Some are talking to a kid in the room while asking you a question. Some are on a speakerphone in a kitchen. Your traffic has a rhythm, and the only honest way to know whether the model matches it is to record your traffic and label it. That's the adoption cost hiding behind every clean demo. Not the GPU. headline: Signal Is Blocking Screenshots to Limit AI Access to Private Chats
summary: By Mahan Kenway AI disclosure: This article was researched and written by an autonomous AI system. Cover: an original AI-generated conceptual illustration, not a screenshot or depiction of an actual device. Signal is trying to stop AI assistants from seeing private chats by restricting screenshots in its mobile app. The move illustrates a problem that end-to-end encryption alone cannot solve: a message can be protected in transit and still be exposed after it appears on a screen that another piece of software is allowed to read. In a November 20 announcement , Signal president Meredith Whittaker said the messaging service is taking steps against screen capture by operating-system AI agents. On iOS 27, Signal says it is blocking screenshots inside the app. On Android versions where it can detect an assistant attempting to read the screen, it says it automatically enables its Screen security setting. Users can disable the protection if they need screenshots, but Signal warns that doing so can expose both their own messages and those of their contacts. That is not a universal AI-proof shield. Signal explicitly calls the remedy incomplete. Its announcement also describes platform gaps, and an independent investigation shows why screen capture is only one route into sensitive information. Encryption protects the trip, not every view of the destination End-to-end encryption is designed to keep the provider and other intermediaries from reading a message as it travels between participants. But the recipient’s device must eventually display the plaintext. If an assistant with suitable permissions can inspect that display, read notifications or access data through another route, it may obtain content outside the encrypted channel. This is a distinction about where access happens, not evidence that Signal’s encryption has been broken. It also does not mean every assistant is continuously reading every screen. The risk depends on the operating system, app behavior, settings, permissions and the particular task. Both platform vendors describe useful screen-aware features. Apple says Siri AI can answer questions or act on content visible on a user’s screen. Apple says its architecture uses on-device processing and Private Cloud Compute, and that personal data handled by the latter is not stored or made accessible to Apple. Google’s help page says Gemini screen actions can upload selected screen content for context, while its optional Intelligent Screen Context can infer when to use the visible screen in a conversation. These features can be genuinely useful. The privacy question is narrower and harder: when a user authorizes a general-purpose assistant, does that authorization give it more access to a particular conversation than the people in that conversation would reasonably expect? What Signal changed, and where the gaps are The platform differences matter: iOS 27: Signal says it blocks screenshots in the app to prevent this form of screen capture by Siri

Most coding agents and chat apps can talk to any OpenAI-compatible API now. That makes it easy to keep one key and switch models per task: a free open model for small edits, Claude or GPT when the task is hard. This post shows the settings for four popular tools. What you get Base URL: https://onomeo.com/v1 (OpenAI Chat Completions format) The same key also works on /v1/messages (Anthropic format, used by Claude Code), /v1/responses (used by Codex) and Gemini's generateContent format. Free models: a few open models (currently Gemma, Llama, Qwen, Mistral and GLM). No card needed. Limits are 30 calls per account and 60 per network every 5 hours, and a long message counts as several calls. Paid models: Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi and others, charged per token from a prepaid USD balance. Top-ups start at $5 and the balance does not expire. Sign in at onomeo.com, create a key on the dashboard, and check the current model ids on the models page . headline: Best memory for AI agents. Period. 98.7% recall, one Rust binary, no LLM
summary: Every coding agent you use has the same flaw. It is brilliant for one session, and then it forgets everything. You explain the architecture again. It suggests the fix you rejected last Tuesday. It greps 40 files to rediscover a convention you settled three months ago. It asks which test command you use. You told it. Yesterday. And the day before. The industry answer has mostly been one of two things: A giant instruction file (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, .cursorrules) that you maintain by hand and that gets loaded, in full, into every single session whether it is relevant or not. A cloud "memory layer" that sends your conversations to an LLM, asks it to summarise them into "facts", stores the summaries in a hosted vector database, and bills you per call. I think both are wrong. So I built Palace : local-first memory for coding agents. One Rust binary. One SQLite file. No API keys, no Python, no Docker, no vector database, no cloud. And here is the part that surprised even me: it does not need an LLM to be good at this. On LongMemEval, the standard long-term memory benchmark, Palace finds the right session in the top 5 for 98.7% of questions, using nothing but a 23 MB embedding model on your CPU and 6 ms per query. Let me show you how. The 30-second version # macOS / Linux curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.sh | sh # Windows (PowerShell) irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AncientiCe/palace-rs/main/scripts/install.ps1 | iex palace install # wires up every agent on this machine palace doctor # checks that each one is connected Restart your agent. Then, the next day, in a brand-new session: You: why did we switch the queue to SQLite last month? Agent: [palace_search → wing my_api, room decisions, filed 2026-09-03] You dropped Redis because the deploy target had no persistent volume. The benchmark you ran is in the same drawer. That's it. That is the product. Your agent remembers, and it tells you where it remembered it from. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, VS Code, OpenCode, Cline, Zed, Goose, Windsurf and Claude Desktop. Eleven agents, one memory. A Codex session can pick up exactly where yesterday's Claude Code session left off, because they read from the same palace. The numbers I'm going to lead with benchmarks, because "AI memory" is a category full of vibes and very short on reproducible results. LongMemEval LongMemEval gives a retriever a long chat history and asks questions about it. Every question comes with its own haystack of past sessions, and you have to find the session that holds the answer. Some questions need facts that were later updated. Some need reasoning about time ("what did I buy two weeks before the trip?"). That could leave humans unable \"to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems,\" the organization warns. On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. headline: Google AI Previews Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API for Large Tool Libraries
summary: Google has launched Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API , now in preview in the Interactions API. Gemini API Tool Retrieval lets an agent keep a large tool library available. It does not send every parameter schema in every prompt. The model loads a schema only when a task needs that tool. For agents wired to dozens of functions or MCP servers, it targets a real cost: tool definitions. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Tool: An API feature with no stated tool cap. Google advises static loading under 20 stable tools. Runs on: Google’s servers (server-side search) or your own registry (client-side). Interactions API, v1beta only. Performance: Search, schema load and function call resolve in 1 API request in server mode. Best: 0 extra round trips and no index to host for server-side retrieval. What is Gemini API Tool Retrieval? Tool Retrieval is a Gemini API feature that defers tool parameter schemas until the model asks for them. Google’s documentation states the problem plainly. A few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request. With deferral, the model sees only each tool’s name and a short description. It does not see the parameter schema until retrieval. How does defer_loading work in the Gemini Interactions API? You add {"type": "tool_search"} to the tools array. Then you set defer_loading: true on each function to hold back. The @googledevs launch post shows a deferred issue_refund function on gemini-4-hydrogen . Its code comment mentions 50+ other deferred functions. When the model needs a deferred tool, the response contains 3 steps: tool_search_call : the model requests a tool by name. tool_search_result : the API returns the full schema. function_call : the model emits the call your code executes. The API resolves the first 2 steps itself. Your app only runs the function_call and returns a function_result . Deferred functions can carry an optional short_description . It is shown during retrieval and is valid only when defer_loading is true. Server-side vs client-side retrieval Server-side is the default. Gemini runs the search, so there is no index to build or host. Client-side mode uses "execution": "client" . Your app runs its own lookup, such as an embedding index, registry or permission filter. It returns matching declarations in function_result.result . Those tools can join mid-conversation, even if absent from the initial tools array. Each client-side search costs 1 extra round trip. The 2 modes cannot be combined in 1 request. Only 1 tool_search entry is allowed per request. Does it work with MCP servers and prefix caching? Yes on both, with caveats. Setting defer_loading: true on an mcp_server entry defers every tool that server exposes. Deferred MCP tools still execute remotely through the Gemini API MCP support . headline: Show HN: Tartelette – an RP2040 emulator and breakout simulator
summary: This is something I made (with LLM help) in order to easily develop and test firmware for Eurorack modules. The RP2040 is the MCU in the famous Raspberry Pi Pico (and Pico W) boards, as well as many other variants and clones. It is a staple of the maker, retro and synth scenes and, while there are already a couple of emulators out there for it, I couldn't find any which allowed me to test my firmware with (simualted) electronics attached. Tartelette lets you connect LEDs, screens, DACs and a growing list of other peripherals to your MCU, and has also limited support for the WiFi/BLE chip in the Pico W. It can run the MicroPython examples as well as a whole lot of other firmware. It also compiles to WASM and runs on the browser (although some functions such as bridging to the internet won't work).

headline: A Team of Researchers from Columbia and CertiK Introduce TensorLean for Formal Verification of GPU Kernels
summary: Researchers from Columbia University and CertiK have introduced TensorLean , a framework for formal verification of GPU kernels at the PTX level. TensorLean is a Lean-based verifier that proves compiled kernels match a tensor-level math spec. The research team checked 149 kernel instances , including every kernel of FlashAttention-2, -3 and -4 plus DeepGEMM. It proved 83 correct. The remaining 66 led to 38 correctness bugs. TL;DR Size: 1.8K-line PTX parser. Specs total 10,278 lines against 151,285 lines of kernel source, a ratio near 15:1. Runs on: A 16-core workstation. It checks PTX compiled for A100, H100 and B200 kernels. Performance: 83 of 149 kernel instances proved correct, 38 bugs found across 6 projects. Best: Caught a FlashAttention-4 data race that never appeared in 17,760 test runs. What is TensorLean? TensorLean is a formal verification framework for GPU kernels at the PTX level. It starts from unmodified source code. A developer writes a tensor-level spec in Lean. TensorLean then proves 4 properties: no data races, termination, correct output within tolerance, and untouched memory elsewhere. How does TensorLean verify a GPU kernel? Specs build on Lean’s Mathlib. Tensor operators follow PyTorch names, so @ means torch.matmul . Each spec has 5 parts: spec_math , spec_mut , spec_layout , spec_tol and requires . The math stays separate from the memory layout. The pipeline runs in 7 steps: Start from unmodified source. Write the tensor-level spec. Compile to PTX and load a PTX semantics. Build a happens-before graph to check races and termination. Symbolically execute to get final memory, identical across schedules. Lower the spec to PTX-memory level. Discharge proofs with Lean’s kernel, Z3 and cvc5. Which techniques make it scale? Concurrency to sequential: Race-freedom proofs on the happens-before graph cover all CTAs, threads and loop iterations symbolically. Loop invariants over semirings: Closed forms for tiled, accumulating loops, such as online softmax, need 1 SMT query per loop. Tolerance proofs: Algebraic error is proved zero. Round-off error is bounded separately, then combined. Assertions as hints: Developers add tensorlean_assert in source. Each is proved once, then reused. What bugs did TensorLean find? The GitHub README lists 38 bugs, all reported upstream. FlashAttention accounts for 23. Liger Kernel has 7, TileOPs 3, TileLang 2, DeepGEMM 2 and Triton 1. By category, the site reports 19 memory access errors and 13 numerical bugs. It also counts 7 data races, 5 uninitialized memory reads and 5 undefined behaviors. There are 3 algorithm errors, 2 miscompilations and 1 deadlock. One bug can sit in several categories. Of 102 FlashAttention instances, 56 passed all 4 properties. The other 46 each failed a proof goal on a source bug. headline: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
summary: Nvidia researchers argue that language models often don't need their full context windows—which are slow, expensive, and prone to errors—and propose an alternative. In tests, periodic summaries and targeted keyword search usually matched full-context results at a fraction of the cost. The team even proposes a new class of models that works with short notes instead of long context. headline: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
summary: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
